courses.title: Object Oriented Programming in C++
courses.description: Jeff Yim's lectures and sample code, one module per week, plus a Midterm module. Runnable C++ in every lesson.

modules.title: Week 1
modules.subtitle: program structure, types, operators, casting, constants, console IO
modules.description: Built from the Week 1 slides and sample code (HelloWorld, AddIntegers, assortedOps, bits, const_vs_constexpr, precisionAndWidth, readName). Ends with a mock quiz and a cheat sheet.

modules.title: Week 2
modules.subtitle: file IO, arrays, random numbers, pointers, references, strings, vectors, new/delete
modules.description: Built from the Week 2 slides, the lecture videos and the Pointers and References practice sheet. A step-by-step memory diagram for pointers and references, a file-cursor simulator, and runnable versions of every slide program. Ends with the practice sheet worked, a mock quiz and a cheat sheet.

modules.title: Week 3
modules.subtitle: classes, constructors, copying, destructors, inheritance, virtual functions, testing, UML
modules.description: Built from both Week 3 decks, the nine sample projects, the Testing review deck and the UML review. A constructor picker, an object-lifetime stepper, shallow-versus-deep copy and virtual-dispatch visualizers, every slide program runnable with its real output, Lab 3's stack with Catch-style tests you can run. Ends with a mock quiz and a cheat sheet.

modules.title: Week 4
modules.subtitle: abstract classes, interfaces, multiple inheritance, the diamond, friends, operator overloading, copy-and-swap
modules.description: Built from both Week 4 decks and the twelve sample projects. An abstract-class checker, a diamond builder that shows one or two grandparents and which constructor ran, a friendship checker, an operator-call rewriter and a copy-and-swap stepper; every program runnable with its real output. Ends with the midterm practice questions worked, a mock quiz and a cheat sheet.

modules.title: Week 5
modules.subtitle: exceptions, assertions, noexcept, coupling and cohesion, SOLID, the Law of Demeter
modules.description: Built from the Week 5 deck and the five exception programs. A catch-clause matcher, a stack-unwinding stepper, the std::exception family tree, a coupling picture you can rearrange, a SOLID violation spotter and a Demeter train-wreck checker; every program runnable with its real output. Ends with the practice-midterm Fraction constructor, a mock quiz and a cheat sheet.

modules.title: Week 6
modules.subtitle: auto, ranged for, the STL: containers, pair and map, set and strict weak ordering, typedefs, the five iterator kinds, algorithms and partition
modules.description: Built from the Week 6 deck and the twelve Week6 programs. A container picker, a begin/end walker, an iterator-operations table that shows what compiles, a strict-weak-ordering checker, a map insert visualizer and a partition stepper; every program runnable with its real output and the three activities worked (cities, the Date operator<, two structures and two algorithms). Ends with a mock quiz and a cheat sheet.

modules.title: Week 7
modules.subtitle: static members, copy elision and return value optimization, the right-left rule, and the midterm review: references, operators, virtual, functions, the copy constructor
modules.description: Built from the Week 7 deck and the Week7 sample programs (static, static_functions, Calculator, StaticCalculator, basic, copy_elision, Inheritance, Inheritance2, oop_multi3, operators, operatorsBasic). Static members, copy elision and RVO with the real outputs, the right-left rule as a stepper, and the instructor's review block condensed with links back to Weeks 2 to 4. Ends with a mock quiz and a one-page sheet.

modules.title: Midterm
modules.subtitle: Oct 29, 3:30 pm, SW03-1710: the practice midterm worked, the theory questions drilled, a double-sided cheat sheet
modules.description: Built from the Midterm Info slides and the COMP 3522 Practice Midterm. Every Part A theory question with a model answer and the lesson that teaches it, every Part B program traced with its verified output, the Fraction questions built up as challenges into one program, a mock midterm in the real format, and the double-sided cheat sheet for Weeks 1 to 7.

courses.title: Applied Probability and Statistics
courses.description: Carl Gladish's lecture units and labs, one module per unit. Live statistics calculators and pencil problems with instant checking.

modules.title: Unit 1
modules.subtitle: descriptive statistics
modules.description: Proportions, centre, variation, Z-scores, empirical rule, Chebyshev, quartiles, boxplots, outliers, skewness, correlation. Built from the Unit 1 notes and Lab 1; ends with the pencil problems, a mock quiz and a formula sheet.

modules.title: Unit 2
modules.subtitle: visualizing data, and Lab 2 grouped statistics
modules.description: Frequency tables, pie and bar charts, stem-and-leaf, the histogram class recipe, cumulative relative frequencies and ogives, scatter plots; Lab 2 favstats, model formulas, percentiles, percent ranks and Z-scores on the quine data. Built from the Unit 2 notes (filled) and the Lab 2 solutions; ends with the pencil problems, a mock quiz and a formula sheet.

modules.title: Unit 3
modules.subtitle: probability and counting, Lab 3 charts in R, Lab 4 simulations
modules.description: Sample spaces, classical and relative-frequency probability, the law of large numbers, the counting rule, permutations and combinations, the complement, addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability and independence on a two-way table, Bayes' rule on a tree; Lab 3's charts of the survey data and Lab 4's sample()/replicate() simulations. Built from the Unit 3 notes, the demo notebook and both lab solutions; every lecture example worked in full, with clickable sample spaces, a counting calculator, a Bayes tree and a simulation lab. Ends with a mock quiz and a formula sheet.

modules.title: Unit 4
modules.subtitle: discrete probability distributions, and Lab 5 conditional probability in R
modules.description: Discrete random variables and their mean and standard deviation, the binomial, hypergeometric, geometric and Poisson distributions with every lecture example worked and checked in R, when to use which, and Lab 5's conditional probabilities on the SFU weather data. Built from the Unit 4 notes, the demo notebook and the Lab 5 notebook; ends with the examples worked, a mock quiz and a formula sheet.

modules.title: Unit 5
modules.subtitle: continuous probability distributions: uniform, normal, exponential
modules.description: Continuous random variables and densities, the uniform bus wait, the normal distribution with the Z table and R, standardizing, percentiles, the Gaussian bit-error example, and the exponential waiting time with its memoryless property. Built from the (unfilled) Unit 5 notes with every example computed and checked in R; a draggable area widget, an interactive Z table, a mock quiz and a formula sheet.

modules.title: Midterm
modules.subtitle: Wed Oct 28, 3:00 pm, SW5-1840, 90 min, paper and calculator: Units 1 to 4, R commands on paper
modules.description: The study order through the four unit modules, the practice midterm worked question by question in the instructor's rounding, R on paper (the d/p/q/r families, inequalities to p-functions, simulation functions) from Labs 6 and 7, the gaps the unit modules skip (expected dollars, the variance shortcut, Poisson across intervals), the sixteen Unit 4 practice problems, two mock midterms in the real format, and the sheet of what the formula sheet gives you versus what you must know cold.

courses.title: Introduction to Data Communications
courses.description: Marco Ho's lectures and exercise sheets, one module per week. Weekly lab quizzes from Week 2 on the previous weeks; each module ends with a mock quiz and a draft of the one-page study note.

modules.title: Week 1
modules.subtitle: data communications, networks, layering, math review
modules.description: Lectures 01a, 01b, 01c and the Math Review lab, with E01 and the sample quiz worked. Quiz 1 scope (01a) plus the layering half of Quiz 2.

modules.title: Week 2
modules.subtitle: physical layer, data and signals
modules.description: Lecture 02: analog and digital signals, sine waves, phase, wavelength, composite signals and bandwidth, bit rate and levels, with E02 worked. The calculation half of Quiz 2.

modules.title: Week 3
modules.subtitle: transmission, impairment, data rate limits
modules.description: Lecture 03: baseband and broadband transmission, attenuation and the decibel, distortion, noise and SNR, Nyquist and Shannon, bandwidth and the bandwidth-delay product, parallel and serial transmission, with E03 worked. Expected scope of Quiz 3.

modules.title: Week 4
modules.subtitle: digital-to-digital conversion, line coding
modules.description: Lecture 04 and the 04a note: data and signal elements, data rate and signal rate, bandwidth of a digital signal, baseline wandering, self-synchronization, DC components, and unipolar NRZ, NRZ-L, NRZ-I, Manchester, differential Manchester and AMI, waveforms to draw and check, with E04 worked. Expected scope of Quiz 4.

modules.title: Week 5
modules.subtitle: analog-to-digital (PCM) and digital-to-analog / analog-to-analog conversion
modules.description: Lectures 05a and 05b: sampling and the Nyquist rate, quantization with the slide's nine-sample table, encoding and bit rate, quantization error, PCM bandwidth; ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM with their bandwidth boxes, constellation diagrams drawn and read, AM, FM and PM with the radio allocations, with E05 worked. Expected scope of Quiz 5.

modules.title: Week 6
modules.subtitle: bandwidth utilization: FDM, WDM, TDM; the data-link layer, MAC addresses and ARP
modules.description: Lectures 06a and 06b: multiplexing a link into channels, FDM with guard bands and the three-voice-channel example, WDM, synchronous TDM frames, slots and rates with both slide examples, multilevel multiplexing, multiple-slot allocation and pulse stuffing, framing bits; the data-link layer's services and sublayers, link-layer addresses that change at every hop, ARP request and reply, and the Alice-to-Bob walk through two routers, with E06 worked. Expected scope of Quiz 6.

modules.title: Week 7
modules.subtitle: error detection and correction; framing, flow and error control
modules.description: Lectures 07a, 07b and the modulo-2 note: block coding, Hamming distance, parity, CRC division and syndromes, the one's-complement checksum in binary and hex, FEC, byte and bit stuffing, flow and error control, Simple and Stop-and-Wait. Item 12 of the midterm review list.

modules.title: Midterm
modules.subtitle: Oct 29, 11:00, 120 minutes: the review list worked, the differences, a formula drill, a mock midterm, four cheat-sheet sides
modules.description: Built from the Suggested Midterm Review Topics, the Sample Quiz Questions, E01 to E06 and the weekly modules. Every review item with the lesson that teaches it and a compute-first check, the flagged differences as written responses, every calculation type mixed, a 120-minute mock in the sample-quiz shapes, and the two double-sided cheat sheets for Weeks 1 to 7.

courses.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
courses.description: Tom Magliery's lectures, one module per lecture. Pseudocode analysis with live basic-operation counters, and quizzes in the real multiple-choice format; each module ends with a mock quiz and a study sheet.

modules.title: Lecture 1
modules.subtitle: algorithm analysis: basic operations, counting, order of growth, big-O
modules.description: Textbook 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 2.1. What an algorithm is, find and fib, counting statements and basic operations with the tie-breakers, setting up sums, best/worst case, orders of growth and Big-O / Ω / Θ. Every slide algorithm and every quiz-style fragment runs in a per-line execution counter. Ends with the practice problems worked, Mock Quiz 1 and a study sheet.

courses.title: Introduction to Operating Systems
courses.description: Rahim Oraji's lecture Parts 1 to 5 (Tanenbaum), one module per Part, plus a Midterm module. Playback animations for every process that unfolds in time (pipelines, cache traces, clock ticks, state transitions, context switches, fork, the eleven steps of a system call) and quizzes in the midterm's T/F + MCQ and written-calculation formats.

modules.title: Part 1
modules.subtitle: introduction: multilevel machines, kernel and user mode, CPU and pipelining, memory and cache, disks, I/O and interrupts, the OS zoo, processes, files, protection
modules.description: Part 1 of Rahim Oraji's lectures (Tanenbaum Ch. 1 and lecture notes), the largest deck and more than half of the practice midterm: the six-level machine from digital logic to high-level language, the OS as software, extended machine and resource manager, kernel versus user mode and the four x86 rings, the CPU's ALU (the B − A example in 8 bits), control unit and fetch-decode-execute, RISC against CISC, pipelining with the car factory (cycle time 2 h, latency 6 h) and superscalar CPUs, multithreading, multicore, multiprocessors and multicomputers, the memory hierarchy, PC, stack pointer and PSW, EFLAGS, cache lines and sets (64 KB ÷ 64 B = 1024 lines, 128 sets), direct mapping CI = MI % lines and the slide's 15-request trace, replacement algorithms, RAM organizations, disks (seek, rotation, transfer rates) and SSDs, device controllers and drivers, busy waiting, interrupts and DMA, the buses, the nine-entry OS zoo, processes, files, i-nodes, mount, pipes and the rwx protection bits. Playback animations for the pipeline, the cache trace and the interrupt; an ALU and an rwx widget. Ends with a mock midterm section and the closed-book recall drill.

modules.title: Part 2
modules.subtitle: OS structures and clocks
modules.description: Part 2 of Rahim Oraji's lectures (Tanenbaum Ch. 1 and 5): the six structures on the agenda and the five taught; the monolithic main program / service procedures / utility procedures with Linux's loadable modules and the hello-world kernel module; Dijkstra's THE layers and MS-DOS; microkernels and MINIX 3; the client-server model; virtual machines, VM/370 with CMS, type 1 and type 2 hypervisors with ESXi and VirtualBox; then clocks: crystal, counter and holding register, one-shot versus square-wave mode, the 500 MHz → 2 nsec → 8.6 sec arithmetic, the clock driver's six duties, time of day in ticks (overflows in 2.274 years) or seconds (136 years), the quantum counter, CPU accounting, the alarm linked list 3 → 4 → 6 → 2 → 1, and watchdog timers. Playback animations for the programmable clock and the alarm list. Ends with a mock midterm section and the closed-book recall drill.

modules.title: Part 3
modules.subtitle: processes
modules.description: Part 3 of Rahim Oraji's lectures (Tanenbaum Ch. 2): a process as a program in execution with its three segments, multiprogramming as rapid switching, the four creation events and four termination conditions, UNIX process groups against Windows handles, the three states and four numbered transitions, the process table entry and the context switch into the PCB, the interrupt skeleton and vector, CPU utilization = 1 − pⁿ with the 80 % / 10-process example, then Linux: the address space, fork() with pids 4508 and 4509, the stripped-down shell, /proc, pstree, ps and top, the ps state letters D I R S T X Z, the Linux state diagram, zombies and orphans. Playback animations for the state transitions, the context switch and fork; a utilization calculator with the RAM-budget and parallel-jobs modes the written midterm uses. Ends with a mock midterm section and the closed-book recall drill.

modules.title: Part 4
modules.subtitle: threads
modules.description: Part 4 of Rahim Oraji's lectures (Tanenbaum Ch. 2): a thread as a flow of execution with its own program counter, registers and stack; the four motivations (10–100 times faster to create than a process); the word processor with three threads and the dispatcher/worker web server with the three ways to construct a server; the classical model's per-process and per-thread items, each thread's own stack and the four thread states; the six Pthreads calls and the instructor's two-thread demo with pstree and /proc/<pid>/task; user-level versus kernel-level threads with their advantages and problems and the slide's comparison table; hybrid many-to-one, one-to-one and many-to-many; Java threads by extending Thread, implementing Runnable and a lambda, and virtual threads; pop-up threads. Ends with a mock midterm section and the closed-book recall drill.

modules.title: Part 5
modules.subtitle: system calls
modules.description: Part 5 of Rahim Oraji's lectures (Tanenbaum Ch. 1 §1.6 and lecture notes): external, internal and software interrupts; what a system call is and why C programs reach it through a procedure library; stdin, stdout and stderr as file descriptors 0, 1, 2 with the read/write demos; the x86 convention (number in EAX, arguments in EBX, ECX, …, int 80h, result in EAX) and the MIPS equivalent; the eleven steps of read(fd, buffer, nbytes) played step by step; the four POSIX tables verbatim; fork's three return values and every fork program on the slides with its real output; execve and the stripped-down shell; link, hard and symbolic links, mount; the UNIX-to-Win32 table; blocking, non-blocking and POSIX asynchronous I/O. Ends with a mock midterm section and the closed-book recall drill.

modules.title: Midterm
modules.subtitle: Oct 26–30 exam week, closed book, LockDown Browser: Parts 1 to 5
modules.description: The instructor's practice midterm, worked: all 74 Part 1 questions grouped by lecture Part with explanations that teach the slide fact behind each one, the five written questions (pipeline rate and delay, CPU utilization from a job timeline with and without multiprogramming, 1 − pⁿ with a RAM budget, two parallel jobs with 50 % I/O wait, a direct-mapped cache trace) asked for your number first and then worked step by step, a mock Part 1 and a mock Part 2 in the real format with new questions, and the closed-book recall drill across all five Parts.

courses.title: Internet Software Architecture
courses.description: Amir Amintabar's lectures 1 to 7, one module per lecture, plus a Midterm module: JavaScript that runs in the page (scope, hoisting, the event loop, promises), HTML previews, XHR and CORS against live endpoints, Node servers, Node to MySQL, diagrams for every figure, and drills in the midterm's what-prints, short-answer and coding formats with a printable cheat sheet.

modules.title: Lecture 1
modules.subtitle: Review: why the web is hard, OOP in JavaScript, the course coding style, DevTools and hosting, HTML, CSS, JavaScript values, scope and hoisting, functions, objects and the DOM, timers, loops and arrays
modules.description: Lecture 1 of Amir Amintabar's COMP 4537 Internet Software Architecture: the web-vs-desktop challenges table and the device-and-network scenarios; classes, extends and super (Vehicle and Car), composition (Car has an Engine) and the Tesla and Ferrari exercise; the course coding style (const first, then let, never var; no hard-coded user-facing strings; one task per function); the seven DevTools regions; shared, VPS, dedicated and cloud hosting, SSL and index.html; the HTML review (DOCTYPE, the DOM tree, elements and attributes, id and class, the four-part URL); the three ways to style, selectors, combinators and specificity; the box model, display, visibility, position and units; JavaScript's four output methods, six primitives, == vs === and the falsy list; var, let and const scope, hoisting and window; functions, parameters and arguments, arrow functions; objects, constructors, Date and typeof; createElement, appendChild, getElementsByTagName, events and prompt; setTimeout and the 1 3 2 event queue; and loop tracing over arrays beyond the slide for the loop quiz. Every program runs in the browser; the box model, scope, DOM and event-queue figures play step by step. Ends with a 30-item mock quiz in the shape of the Learning Hub quizzes.

modules.title: Lecture 2
modules.subtitle: Architectural patterns, JSON and Web Storage: monolithic, layered and microservices, the course's API-centric architecture, JSON.stringify and JSON.parse, localStorage and sessionStorage
modules.description: Lecture 2 of Amir Amintabar's Internet Software Architecture: architecture as the interaction/relation among components and the decisions made before code; the qualities patterns help evaluate (efficiency, maintenance, development and extension, robustness, security, modularity, deployment cost); monolithic, layered n-tier (presentation, business, application, data access) and microservices with their pros and cons; reliability vs robustness vs resilience; the course's simplified API-centric microservice architecture with an API gateway, services on different machines and JSON responses; the course outcomes; JSON as the serialized payload with JSON.stringify and JSON.parse; HTML Web Storage: localStorage vs sessionStorage, per-origin scope, the four localStorage calls, strings only, objects through JSON, the writer.html / reader.html pair, the DevTools Application tab and where data should and should not live. Diagrams of every pattern, a live storage simulator and editable writer and reader pages. Ends with a 20-item mock quiz.

modules.title: Lecture 3
modules.subtitle: Why API servers exist, the four parts of a web API, GET vs POST, Postman, and REST's constraints with the microservice gateway
modules.description: Lecture 3 of Amir Amintabar's COMP 4537: the review programs (var, let and const scope, the A/B/C hoisting scenarios, the 1 3 2 event-queue script) as predicts; why a monolithic web server that returns rendered HTML pages is a problem for other programs, told through the online movie store, IMDb scraping and the OMDb API server that returns JSON; the API as a documented contract; the anatomy of a web API (headers, data, endpoint, HTTP methods GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) shown on live requests to the app's echo endpoint; the full GET vs POST comparison table (cache, history, bookmark, the 2048-character URL, ASCII only, neither is secure); testing an API with Postman and httpbin; REST as an architectural style, microservices behind an API gateway, and the five RESTful constraints with their principle, benefit and example, plus Code-on-Demand. Ends with a 20-item mock quiz.

modules.title: Lecture 4
modules.subtitle: Servers and Node.js: what a server is, PHP's four steps against Node's three, the restaurant analogy, modules with require and exports, the http, url and fs built-in modules
modules.description: Lecture 4 of Amir Amintabar's COMP 4537: a server as a computer running 24/7 reachable over the internet, the client / web server / DB server / file server / mail server figure, what a server-side script can do, Node.js as an open-source cross-platform JavaScript runtime on Chrome V8, how PHP or ASP handles a file request in four steps and Node.js in three, the restaurant analogy (one non-blocking waiter, one blocking waiter, one waiter per table) and the 100-requests-100-threads figure; then VS Code debugging, the area examples and their wrong formulas, a math.js module loaded with require('./modules/math'), the http server with createServer, writeHead(200, ...), write, end and listen(8888), Access-Control-Allow-Origin, url.parse(adr, true) with host, pathname, search and query, the ?name=John server, and the fs file server with its 404 branch. A playback of the three restaurants and of a request passing through createServer's callback; every Node listing pinned with the output the slide shows. Ends with a 20-item mock quiz in the shape of Quiz 7.

modules.title: Lecture 5
modules.subtitle: AJAX with XMLHttpRequest, the GET demos, CORS and the Same-Origin Policy, POST bodies read in chunks, and connecting Node to MySQL
modules.description: Lecture 5 of Amir Amintabar's deck: sending requests from inside a page with XMLHttpRequest in four steps (create the object, set onreadystatechange, open(method, url, async), send()), readyState 0 to 4 (UNSENT, OPENED, HEADERS_RECEIVED, LOADING, DONE) with the Lecture 6 correction of the w3schools table, the status groups 2xx 3xx 4xx 5xx, Demo 1 and Demo 2 against a Node server on port 8888 run live against the app's echo endpoint, the CORS error and the Same-Origin Policy (origin = protocol + domain + port), Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods and Allow-Headers, the OPTIONS preflight and which content types trigger it, POST with application/x-www-form-urlencoded and a server that collects data chunks and answers on end, then CRUD, XAMPP and phpMyAdmin, npm install mysql, createConnection, connect, query and the INSERT of elon musk with 2900. Playback animations for the XHR lifecycle and the browser's CORS check; every request demo runs for real, including the one CORS blocks. Ends with a 20-item mock quiz in the shape of Quiz 10.

modules.title: Lecture 6
modules.subtitle: Promises: idempotent PUT vs POST vs PATCH, callbacks, the three states, the executor, the event-loop order of Examples 1 to 12, chaining with then, catch and finally, async and await
modules.description: Lecture 6 of Amir Amintabar's course: a review of HTTP verbs (PUT replaces, PATCH updates a property, PUT is idempotent and POST is not), first-class functions and callbacks, why a function doing asynchronous work needs both a value and an outcome, then the JavaScript Promise: the boss-and-raise analogy, pending, fulfilled and rejected (fulfilled and rejected are settled), the annotated constructor with its five notes, the executor running immediately, settle-once, Promise.resolve, and the deck's Examples 1 to 12 with their log orders (synchronous code, then microtasks, then timers). Then chaining (returning a value fulfils the next promise, throwing rejects it), .catch as .then(null, f), .finally, unhandled rejections, the DevTools views of a promise before and after 5 seconds, async and await, two successive AJAX calls and callback hell, GET vs POST response size and the corrected readyState table. Event-loop and promise-chain playbacks for every example; twelve new output-order programs; a 30-item mock quiz.

modules.title: Lecture 7
modules.subtitle: Databases for API development: tables and keys, CRUD from Node.js to MySQL, reading SQL
modules.description: Lecture 7 of Amir Amintabar's COMP 4537: what a database and a DBMS are and the eight DBMS properties, relational (SQL) against NoSQL, a clinic's patient spreadsheet redesigned as Patient and Visit tables joined by Patient_ID, primary and foreign keys, 1:M, 1:1 and M:M through an associative table with a composite primary key, schema against data, the popular MySQL data types, referential integrity, AUTO_INCREMENT and CHECK. Then the part the midterm examines: a Node.js API server that connects to MySQL with the mysql module, creates its table if it does not exist, INSERTs on POST and SELECTs on GET through the (err, result) callback, serves a page on another origin with CORS headers, and follows the principle of least privilege with a SELECT-only database user (a bookstore's books table, in the shape of Lab 5). Ends with a reading reference for the lecture's SQL (WHERE operators, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN, ORDER BY, aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING, subqueries, the cross product) and a 15-item mock quiz in the shape of Quiz 11.

modules.title: Midterm
modules.subtitle: Exam week Oct 26–30: two hours on the Learning Hub, one double-sided letter cheat sheet; lectures 1 to 6 in full and the Node-to-MySQL part of lecture 7
modules.description: The midterm in its own four question kinds. The rules and scope with a strategy for each kind; twenty new what-prints programs on timers, scope, hoisting, promises, chaining and async/await, each run in the browser after you commit to an answer; a short-answer bank (REST's constraints, GET vs POST, CORS and preflight, blocking vs non-blocking, localStorage vs sessionStorage, idempotency, readyState, monolith vs microservices, the four XHR steps, PHP's four steps vs Node's three) with key points to tick; coding questions (a Node server that returns the date in blue, an XHR GET, a callback rewritten as a promise chain, CORS headers, a query string); two forty-item mock midterms in the exam's mix; the cheat sheet as a lesson and a print-ready letter page; and a closed-book recall drill of every fixed list in the course.

courses.title: Ethics for Computing Professionals
courses.description: Vasco Castela's lectures 1 to 5, one module per lecture, plus a Midterm module: moral reasoning drills, Kohlberg's stages, relativism and objectivism, act utilitarianism I and II, every listed practice question answered in writing against a marker's checklist, two mock midterms and a printable answer-skeleton sheet.

modules.title: Lecture 4
modules.subtitle: Act utilitarianism I: from relativism to theories, the hats of hacking, Bentham, equal consideration of interests, the felicific calculus, Mill, the utilitarian procedure, and Jim, the trolley, the fat man, Strangelove and Andy
modules.description: Lecture 4 of LIBS 7102: why rejecting relativism needs a normative theory and why "it depends" is not relativism; white, black and grey hats and what utilitarianism looks at; Bentham's two sovereign masters, psychological and normative hedonism and the principle of utility; equal consideration of interests and the five-person row, not the majority; the seven dimensions of the felicific calculus and why no kind of action is wrong in itself; Mill's four changes, the Greatest Happiness Principle read correctly, the competent judges and the proof; how a utilitarian can know what to do; Williams's Jim, the trolley, the fat man, Strangelove's ICBM and Andy's lie, each put to you before the verdict. Practice answer U3 and a 20-item mock quiz.

modules.title: Lecture 5
modules.subtitle: Act utilitarianism II: dark patterns and Canadian law, how not to describe utilitarianism, Mill's three objections, Nozick and the proof, aggregation, negative responsibility, promises, punishment, justice, and Singer on impartiality and supererogation
modules.description: Lecture 5 of LIBS 7102: dark patterns, the FTC, the EU and Canada's PIPEDA, CASL and Bill C-27; consent and avuncular ethics; the essay revisions: not "for the majority", not cost-benefit, not "right because it causes happiness", the three-step procedure and why it is act utilitarianism; the doctrine of swine, too high for humanity and lack of time with Mill's replies and Sandel's doctors; psychological and normative hedonism, Nozick's experience machine and Mill's proof; aggregating utility, the strong doctrine of negative responsibility, trivial actions and the dying man's promise; rehabilitation, deterrence and vengeance, and Peter and Sarah's pay; Singer's Famine, Affluence and Morality, impartiality, the three kids and the threshold of supererogation; the fourteen objections. Practice answers U1, U2, U4 to U15 and a 22-item mock quiz.
